To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the climbing fiber system is a gain control system for parallel fiber synapses, which is based on a complex interplay of presynaptic and postsynaptic signaling mechanisms.

complex spike activity induces postsynaptic LTD at parallel fiber synapse and presynaptic LTD at climbing fiber synapses by a retrograde cannabinoid signal, while the release of CRF facilitates both forms of LTD.
climbing fiber signals adjust the gain of cerebellar learning by controlling postsynaptic LTD versus LTP induction at parallel fiber-PG synapses and by modulating CRF-mediated LTD induction.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question how climbing fiber signaling controls the gain of synaptic plasticity in the parallel fiber-Purkinge cell synapse and how climbing fiber plasticity contributes to the fine-tuning of this control.
how the complex spike signal, which has been the focus of cerebellar research for decades, contributes to cerebellar gain control.
the role of climbing fibers in cerebellar physiology and motor learning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
climbing fiber activity provides a gain control mechanism that adjusts the relative probabilities for LTD and LTP at parallel fiber synapse.
climbing fiber signaling controls the gain of cerebellar learning, but the exact mechanism of how it does so still has to be determined.
climbing fiber signaling controls the gain of cerebellar LTD induction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
climbing fiber signaling provides a gain control of parallel fiber signaling by controlling the induction of LTD.
climbing fiber signaling adjusts gain control in the cerebellum by controlling LTD/LTP induction at parallel fiber synapse and by controlling CRF-mediated plasticity.

the cerebellar climbing fiber system provides a means to adjust the gain control of parallel fiber-Purkinge cell synapses, and that the gain of this gain control is adjusted by the plasticity of the climbing fibers themselves.
The main takeaway from our work is that
climbing fiber signaling does not only provide a gain control mechanism, but also allows for the fine-tuning of this mechanism.
the complex spike is not just the trigger of LTD, but a key component of the cerebellar gain control system.
climbing fiber signaling provides an additional layer of control over cerebellar gain and plasticity, but does not seem to be essential for learning and motor control.
